title: Right-Mind and Wrong-Mind (简体中文)

full_text:
In a prosperous city lived two companions named Dharmabuddhi, or Right-Mind, and Dushtabuddhi, or Wrong-Mind. Right-Mind was honest, virtuous, and hardworking, while Wrong-Mind was lazy, envious, and perpetually scheming to live upon the toil of others.

One day, Wrong-Mind proposed: 'Friend, why waste our youth in this city? Let us travel to distant foreign lands, trade with courage, and acquire vast riches so that we may live in comfort in our old age.'

Agreeing to the proposal, Right-Mind set out with him. Through honest enterprise, keen commercial foresight, and diligence, they amassed a fortune of one thousand pure gold dinars and returned toward their native city.

As they reached the forest outskirts, Right-Mind proposed: 'Let us divide our gold equally, five hundred dinars to each, and enter the city rejoicing.'

Wrong-Mind, plotting to steal the whole treasure, said: 'Friend, it is dangerous to carry so much gold into the town; thieves, relatives, and tax collectors will torment us. Let us take one hundred dinars each for immediate expenses, and bury the remaining eight hundred dinars beneath the roots of this ancient, hollow banyan tree. Whenever we need more gold, we will return together and unearth it.'

Trusting his friend, Right-Mind agreed. They buried the eight hundred gold coins in a deep pit beneath the banyan and entered the city.

A few nights later, Wrong-Mind stole into the forest under the cover of darkness, dug up the treasure, pocketed all eight hundred dinars, refilled the pit with earth, and returned home.

A month later, Wrong-Mind approached Right-Mind, saying: 'Brother, my funds are exhausted; let us go to the banyan and divide the remaining gold.'

They dug beneath the roots, but found only an empty pit!

In an instant, Wrong-Mind tore his hair, beat his chest, and screamed: 'Thief! Traitor! You came by night and stole our eight hundred dinars! Divide the gold with me, or I will drag you before the King's magistrates!'

Right-Mind was stunned: 'I have never touched the gold! My name is Right-Mind, and I would rather die than commit a theft!'

They dragged the dispute before the city court. When the judges, unable to decide between their conflicting oaths, ordered the trial by ordeal of fire, Wrong-Mind said: 'Why resort to divine ordeals when a living witness is at hand? The sacred spirit of the banyan tree witnessed our burial of the gold! Let the judges come to the tree tomorrow at dawn and hear the witness of the tree!'

That night, Wrong-Mind concealed his aged father inside the hollow trunk of the banyan tree, instructing him: 'When the judges ask who stole the gold, cry out with a loud voice: "Right-Mind is the thief!"'

At dawn, the magistrates assembled around the banyan. The chief judge called out: 'O sacred Tree Spirit! Reveal the truth: who took the eight hundred gold dinars?'

From the hollow trunk, a trembling voice boomed: 'Hearken, O judges! Right-Mind is the thief who dug up the gold!'

The judges were astounded and prepared to condemn Right-Mind to the gallows.

Right-Mind, however, suspected foul play. Pondering the hollow trunk, he said calmly: 'Before sentence is passed, allow me to perform a sacred purification ritual to honor this miraculous tree spirit.'

Gathering dry thorns, brushwood, and heaps of dry leaves, Right-Mind piled them around the entrance of the hollow trunk and set the brush on fire, fanning the dense, acrid smoke into the cavity.

Within moments, agonizing shrieks echoed from within the trunk. Out tumbled Wrong-Mind's aged father, his clothes on fire, his skin blistered, coughing up blood and soot. Falling before the judges, the dying man confessed the entire criminal conspiracy orchestrated by his wicked son.

The judges condemned Wrong-Mind to be hanged upon the nearest tree, while Right-Mind was awarded the recovered gold and the praise of the entire kingdom.

Thus Vishnu Sharma taught:
"The knave who weaves an evil plot and uses sacred names,
And hides his fraud behind a tree, shall perish in the flames;
For truth unmasks the deepest plot that wicked minds devise,
And justice turns the scheming trap against the lord of lies."
moral: Truth and righteousness triumph over deceit; he who uses his own father in fraud brings ruin upon his house. [ZH]

quiz.question: What is the central moral lesson taught in "Right-Mind and Wrong-Mind"?
options: True wealth lies in contentment and honesty; greed leads to ruin.
Acting in haste and anger without thinking
Believing rumors and flattery without proof
quiz.hint: Remember the moral lesson of this traditional story.

quiz.question: How do the characters overcome their challenge?
options: Through patience, calm reflection, and wisdom
By shouting loudly and blaming others
By running away from every problem
quiz.hint: Consider the virtues praised in world folklore.

quiz.question: What memorable conclusion does this story teach young readers?
options: Honesty, kindness, and clear thinking lead to peace
quiz.hint: Reflect upon the resolution of the story.

discussion_questions.prompt: What is the main situation at the beginning of "Right-Mind and Wrong-Mind"?
Why does this story teach that "True wealth lies in contentment and honesty; greed leads to ruin."?
How could you use this lesson in your own school or family life?
Was the character’s final decision fair and kind to everyone?
Imagine an alternate peaceful ending or a new creative adventure for these characters.

reflection_prompt: Have you ever had to choose between acting quickly in anger or waiting patiently to understand the truth?
